pillar_reactions.evidence: Immediately after the three-step training explanation the prospect said 'That's like, this is exactly what I'm interested in.' He had already tied the modality to his own goal earlier — 'I like the idea that you use your body as leverage ... this idea of being grounded and anchored, like your feet are attached to the floor' — and the rep's 'we're not going to throw you into the deep end and just give you like a 60-pound kettlebell to start pressing over your head' spoke directly to his disclosed fear of the overhead press.

'I really concur and resonate with all the philosophy behind your program.' He also tied it back to his own words: 'that's maybe whenever I said simplicity, I kept referring to like this simplistic, almost like ancient human ... that's why I was attracted because it's just like, it's really in tune with it.' Note he pushed gently on the mechanism — 'if you want to lose weight, there must be like a calorie deficit, right?' — and the rep reframed rather than contradicted.

He asked repeatedly to understand the mechanics rather than reacting to the value: 'so you mentioned that like the educational process is sort of all through this app ... I'm guessing it's through video', 'so just like they're hosted through the app', and 'just through a week, it would just be ... are you given like a sort of schedule ... what does that look like throughout the week?' His summary at the end was mechanical, not motivational: 'you have like a database, which is like the school platform, and then an app platform.'

anchors.raw: I could I was like man I hope it costs like 500 a month like I feel like that's fair because like um whatever like go to like gyms like the like just like what a gym membership cost what a private instruction cost I felt like I was like that's what I was like shooting for in my head
anchors.competitor: Local gyms / conventional private personal training
anchors.note: He arrived with no prior coaching experience at all ('I've never actually done personal training before'), so his only reference point was a gym membership plus private instruction. That set an internal ceiling of $500-600/month before he heard $1,000/month, and he stated the ceiling twice — 'okay, maybe $500 a month, $600 a month would be doable. But that seems a bit of a stretch for me.' The rep had actually pre-framed the range early ('if your budget's like 50 bucks a month ... if you have a couple grand') but never converted that into a qualifying question.

anchors.raw: there was a sort of simplicity in Trevor's, like, guidance and the way that he approached things, and I found that simplicity to be very elegant, and I've been trying to follow along with, like, the bits and, like, the sort of breadcrumb trail on the digital breadcrumb trail
anchors.note: Proposed label: free_content_of_the_same_provider. He is already self-serving from Trevor's free material and already owns the kettlebells and the mace. That cuts both ways — it is warm intent that supports paying, but it is also a functioning zero-cost substitute he can keep using, and he named exactly that as his fallback at the end.

unmet_demand.want: A monthly entry point into one-to-one coaching at or under about $500-600/month, reachable by someone pre-revenue
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The published offer starts at $6,000 for six months. The rep improvised down to $650/month over 12 months and then to a $4,000 three-month tier, and still could not reach the prospect's stated ceiling; the only thing at his price was Primal University, which is explicitly not one-to-one with Trevor.

unmet_demand.want: Guidance on whether the mace he already bought is the right one — 'I think I maybe got the wrong mace ... it feels maybe too long, and it's a little maybe too heavy. And I am, I have no idea if I'm doing the right thing with it at all.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The rep confirmed the mace is coached ('Yeah, I want to learn the mace' → covered) but never addressed the equipment-fit question, which was the actual thing asked.
